name: Hirudo medicinalis (leech therapy)

lead: Hirudo medicinalis is the European medicinal leech, used in medicine for thousands of years and revived in the 1970s in microsurgery. In plastic and reconstructive surgery a leech is placed on a flap or reattached part, such as an ear, lip, nose, eyelid or finger, to draw off pooled blood and keep tissue alive when veins are not draining it.

For appearance, the payoff is indirect: it helps a surgical repair survive so the reconstructed feature looks as intended. Leeches have also been used or marketed in traditional and complementary medicine for pain and skin conditions, with small trials in osteoarthritis and tennis elbow.

paras: In hospitals, a trained team applies the leech to the congested area, where it feeds and the wound keeps oozing afterwards because of anticoagulant compounds in its saliva. Nursing guidance covers handling and housing the animals. Outside hospitals, practitioners of complementary medicine offer leech sessions for pain and circulation complaints; that use is separate from the surgical one.

The most common complication is prolonged bleeding. Bacterial infection and allergic reactions can also occur. In the United States the FDA classified leeches as medical devices in 2004. Anyone considering it outside a clinical setting is directed by health services to a licensed provider.

angle.text: Leech therapy is used within plastic and reconstructive surgery to rescue tissue that could otherwise be lost, protecting the cosmetic result of a repair. It is a supporting treatment applied by clinicians, not a standalone cosmetic procedure.

lead: Hirudo medicinalis, the European medicinal leech, is a freshwater annelid used in medicine for millennia. Leech therapy has been recorded in ancient Egypt around 3,500 years ago and in Greek, Sanskrit, early Chinese and Arabic medical texts.[1][2] After falling out of favour late in the nineteenth century, it returned in the 1970s, mainly in microsurgery.[1][3]

Its modern, best-documented use is salvaging tissue threatened by venous congestion after reconstructive surgery or replantation: fingers, ears, noses, lips and eyelids.[1][3][4] That connects to appearance because it helps repaired facial features and skin grafts survive.

Leech saliva contains about 60 proteins, among them the anticoagulant hirudin, platelet aggregation inhibitors and vasodilators, according to Wikipedia.[1] Small randomized trials have also looked at leech therapy or saliva extract for knee osteoarthritis and chronic tennis elbow.[5][6]
infobox: Classified as a medical device by the FDA in 2004[1]

paras: Leeches were used to remove blood under humoral medicine, which held that excess blood caused fever and inflammation. Demand in the nineteenth century was large: Wikipedia notes Manchester Royal Infirmary used about 50,000 leeches in 1831, and wild populations are now scattered and legally protected across most of their range.[1] Reviews describe use by ancient Egyptian, Indian, Greek and Arab physicians for conditions from skin disease to nervous system abnormalities.[2]

Wikipedia describes the benefit as coming mainly from continued bleeding after the leech detaches, together with the anaesthetic, anti-inflammatory and vasodilating properties of its saliva; the blood the leech itself takes is small.[1] Hirudin is too scarce in leeches to harvest, so hirudin and related substances are produced by recombinant methods, and 'mechanical leeches' delivering heparin have been developed but are not commercially available.[1]

A 2003 review concluded leeches are used successfully for only a few conditions today, notably salvaging flaps and grafts threatened by venous congestion in microsurgery, and suggested hirudin's anticoagulant properties might lead to wider use.[3] A 2009 nursing review described the resurgence in plastic and reconstructive surgery and gave guidelines for safe administration.[4]

Randomized trials outside surgery are small. A trial of a liposomal gel of leech saliva extract for knee osteoarthritis assessed symptoms over 30 days with Lequesne and VAS questionnaires;[5] a randomized trial of 40 patients with chronic lateral epicondylitis tested a single treatment with locally applied leeches.[6] A 2017 review summarised possible modes of action across several diseases.[7]

Wikipedia lists prolonged bleeding as the most common complication, easily treated, with serious allergic reactions and bacterial infections also occurring.[1] Nursing guidance emphasises training in administering the therapy and maintaining the animals.[4] The US FDA classified medicinal leeches as a medical device in 2004.[1]
